This page introduces a file format for the data of a Perturb-seq screen: the
counts, and what is known about the cells and the gRNAs. It is written for
someone who has not seen the format before.

The format does not invent a container. It is a set of names and rules on top
of [MuData](https://mudata.readthedocs.io), an existing file format for cells
measured in several ways. It is meant for any software that handles
Perturb-seq data, and nothing in it is specific to one analysis tool. The
[sceptre analysis format](https://raw.githack.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/main/sceptre-analysis-format/overview.html), which
stores sceptre's analyses of such a file, is separate and builds on this one:
an analysis names its data file by the dataset identifier that the file
carries.

**If you are reviewing.** Comments are wanted most on the
[open questions](#open-questions) at the end, and this page is meant to be
enough to answer them. The rules themselves, numbered, are in
[`SPEC.md`](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/SPEC.md), and the reasons
for each, with evidence, are in
[`RATIONALE.md`](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/RATIONALE.md); read
those to check a detail. A label such as S8 on this page is the number of a
group of rules, the same in both documents.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Draft.** Nothing here has been reviewed. The format is version 0.1 until it
is frozen as 1.0, and anything in it can still change. No released version of
sceptre or of pysceptre, its Python counterpart, reads or writes it yet: adopting it in the packages and
the pipeline is the next phase of the [roadmap](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import overview_tools as nt

nt.SCREEN = Path("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
nt.screen_spec = spec = json.loads(Path("spec/screen.json").read_text())
counts = nt.rule_counts("SPEC.md")
conforming = sum(c["conforms"] for c in nt.cases())
broken = len(nt.cases()) - conforming
```

## At a glance

A data file is one MuData file, with the extension `.h5mu`. MuData holds one
set of cells measured in several ways. Each kind of measurement is a
**modality**, and each modality has three parts: a count matrix (`X`), a table
with one row per cell (`obs`), and a table with one row per feature (`var`).
The file also has a cell table shared by all modalities, and a place for
entries about the file as a whole (`uns`).

<pre class="layout">
screen.h5mu
├── mod/
│   ├── rna/        one modality for each thing measured
│   │   ├── X       counts, cells × features
│   │   ├── obs     this modality's cell table
│   │   └── var     its feature table: one row per gene
│   └── grna/       the gRNA modality, always under this name
│       ├── X       gRNA counts, cells × gRNAs
│       ├── obs
│       └── var     the gRNA table: one row per gRNA
├── obs             the cell table shared by all modalities
└── uns             entries about the file as a whole
</pre>

For someone who knows sceptre, this is where its inputs end up:

| In sceptre today | In a data file |
|---|---|
| The response matrix | The counts of a modality named for what was measured, usually `rna` |
| The gRNA matrix | The counts of the modality `grna` |
| `grna_target_data_frame` | The gRNA table: `grna_target`, and the optional `target_chr`, `target_start`, `target_end` and `vector_id`. The gRNA's identifier is the row name |
| The covariates sceptre computes (`response_n_umis`, `grna_n_nonzero`, ...) | `n_umis`, `n_nonzero` and `p_mito` in each modality's cell table. They are optional |
| A covariate recorded with the experiment, such as batch or lane | A column of the shared cell table |
| `extra_covariates` given for an analysis | Not in the data file. They are stored with the analysis |
| `moi` | Not in the data file. It is a setting of an analysis |
| Assignments, quality control, results | Not in the data file. They are an analysis |

The rest of the page has five parts: the **principles** every choice follows
from, a **specification overview**, an **example** file opened up, **native
reading** with standard libraries, and **validation**: how a file, and the
format itself, is checked.

## Principles

Every choice in the format follows from these eight. Where two of them pull
apart, the earlier one wins. Open one for its reason and what follows from it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.principles("RATIONALE.md", "https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/RATIONALE.md", "## 2. The eight principles"))
```

## Specification overview

MuData says how matrices and tables are encoded. This format says which ones a
Perturb-seq file has, what they are called, and what they may contain.

| Part | Rules | In brief |
|---|---|---|
| Modalities | S2 | A modality named `grna` and at least one other, each named for what was measured (`rna`, `protein`). All hold the same cells in the same order |
| Counts | S3, S4 | Raw integer counts, cells × features, sparse, stored feature by feature, as 32-bit integers |
| Cell tables | S5 to S7 | What was recorded about each cell with the experiment (batch, lane, donor) is in the shared table. What was measured in one modality is in that modality's table. Only a few kinds of column are allowed, listed below |
| gRNA table | S8 | `grna_target` for every gRNA, with `non-targeting` for a control. Optionally the target's position, the vector that delivers the gRNA, and the kind of gRNA |
| Identifiers | S9 | Every cell has a unique identifier. Every feature has one that is unique across the modalities of the file |
| The file's own entries | S10 | The format version and an identifier for the dataset. Optionally a title, the organism, the genome build, the kind of perturbation and a source |
| Compression | S11 | None or gzip, as the writer chooses |
| What is left out | S12 | Anything an analysis chooses or produces. The file is written once. Changing the data means writing a new file |

The three tables below are read from `spec/screen.json`, the machine-readable
part of the specification.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Columns of a modality's cell table</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.definitions(spec["cell_tables"]["every_modality"], "Column"))
```

- Other columns are allowed, in this table and in the shared one. A column
  name starts with a letter and has only letters, digits, underscores and
  dots.
- **Kinds of column.** In a cell table: a decimal number, a 32-bit whole
  number, or a categorical (a factor). In a feature table, which includes the
  gRNA table: the same, or text. True/false columns, 64-bit whole numbers and
  text columns in a cell table are not allowed, because one of the two
  languages does not read them back correctly. A covariate that is text is
  stored as a categorical.
- A missing value is `NaN` in a decimal column and a missing level in a
  categorical.
- `p_mito` is computed when the file is written, by whoever knows which genes
  are mitochondrial. The format defines no annotation of genes.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Columns of the gRNA table</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.definitions(spec["grna_table"], "Column"))
```

- **The gRNA's identifier** is the row name of the table, as the cell's
  identifier is the row name of a cell table.
- **A target position** is 1-based with both ends included, as in a GTF file.
  A file with positions must give the genome build. Positions are on the
  genome: a screen that targets RNA names the transcript in `grna_target` and
  leaves positions out. They may be stored as whole or as decimal numbers; the
  example stores them as decimal numbers.
- **A vector** is the construct that delivers gRNAs into a cell. Some
  libraries put several gRNAs against one target on one vector. `vector_id`
  says which gRNAs travel together. Where the column is present every gRNA has
  a value, and a gRNA delivered alone has a vector of its own. All gRNAs of a
  vector must have the same target; a library that combines different targets on one vector is outside
  this version of the format.
- **The kinds of gRNA.** `targeting` is an ordinary gRNA. The other three are
  controls: `non-targeting` matches nothing in the genome, `safe-targeting`
  cuts at a site believed to have no effect, and `negative control` is any
  other control. Every control, of whichever kind, has `grna_target` equal to
  `non-targeting`. So the word `non-targeting` appears in two columns: as the
  target of every control, and as the kind of one sort of control. A control
  may have a position: for a safe-targeting gRNA, where it cuts. A positive control is a `targeting` gRNA: which pairs
  serve as positive controls is a choice of an analysis.
- **Not stored:** sceptre's `grna_group`, the grouping of gRNAs that an
  analysis tests together. It depends on how the analysis combines gRNAs.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Entries of <code>uns</code></summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.definitions([{"name": k, **v} for k, v in spec["metadata"]["entries"].items()], "Entry"))
```

`dataset_id` is assigned when a file is first written from the raw data. A
copy of the file keeps it. Data that is imported again, or corrected, is a new
dataset and gets a new one.

`uns` may hold entries of other tools. They are not the format's, and software
reading the file ignores them. In R the entries are in `metadata()` of the
object that is read.

</details>

### Versions

A file carries the version of the format it follows, `perturb_seq_format`, in
two parts: `MAJOR.MINOR`. A minor increase adds something older software can
ignore. A major increase is any change after which older software could
misread a file, and software refuses a file whose major version it does not
know. Version 0 is the draft: until 1.0, rules can change without notice.

### The choices behind it

These are the choices that cannot change after the format is frozen without
breaking existing files. Each opens to its reason and the alternative it was
chosen over.

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The data is one MuData <code>.h5mu</code> file.</strong> <span class="where">S1</span></summary>

- **Why.** MuData is the standard of scverse, the Python single-cell ecosystem that scanpy belongs to, for one set of cells measured in several ways. Bioconductor reads and writes it too. Standard libraries open it in both languages, and one file is easy to move and publish.
- **Instead of.** A Zarr store, two `.h5ad` files, the `ondisc` format, or a folder of Parquet and matrix files. `RATIONALE.md`, S1, compares them.
- **Locks in.** HDF5. A Zarr variant could be added later without changing anything else.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Data and analysis are separate.</strong> <span class="where">S12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The data file holds nothing an analysis produces: no assignments, no kept-or-removed flag, no results. Analyses are stored apart from it.
- **Why.** One dataset has many analyses, and the data file is then written once and never touched again. Keeping a kept-or-removed flag in the data file, as pysceptre (the Python implementation of sceptre) does, means rewriting the whole file to work on the kept cells.
- **Instead of.** One self-contained file holding data, assignments and results, which is the layout of the IGVF consortium's Perturb-seq pipeline and suits uploading one file to a portal.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Counts are stored by feature.</strong> <span class="where">S3</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The count matrix is cells × features, column-compressed, so one gene is one contiguous read.
- **Why.** Fitting a model goes gene by gene. With counts stored by cell, the IGVF consortium's pipeline first splits the whole file into per-gene chunk files.
- **Cost.** A file from another tool is usually stored by cell and is converted once at import.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Modalities are named for what was measured.</strong> <span class="where">S2</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The gRNA modality is always `grna`. Every other modality is named for its measurement (`rna`, `protein`, ...). The file marks none as the one to analyse.
- **Why.** A file can then hold a second measured modality, and any of them can be analysed later.
- **Instead of.** A name for the part a modality plays in an analysis, such as `response`.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Facts about the cell are in the shared cell table, measurements in each modality's own.</strong> <span class="where">S5</span></summary>

- **The choice.** Facts about the cell (batch, donor) are in the shared cell table. Measurements of a modality (`n_umis`) are in that modality's cell table, under their plain names. No shared column starts with a modality's name and an underscore, so software that sets the tables side by side under prefixed names (`rna_n_umis`) gets distinct names.
- **Why.** A batch belongs to the cell, not to its RNA.
- **Instead of.** Everything in one modality's cell table, or everything in the shared table.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The file's own entries are at the top level of <code>uns</code>.</strong> <span class="where">S10</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The format version (`perturb_seq_format`), the dataset's identifier (`dataset_id`) and what is known about the screen (`title`, `organism`, `genome_build`, `perturbation_type`, `source`) are scalar entries at the top level of `uns`.
- **Why.** They are facts about the dataset, so other tools should be able to read and write them. Under a key named for one tool they would belong to that tool.
- **Not in the file.** Whether a screen is treated as low or high multiplicity of infection. It is a choice about how to analyse a screen, so it belongs with the analysis.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The names.</strong> <span class="where">S2 to S10</span></summary>

Names are as hard to change as structure: the modality names `rna` and `grna`, and the columns `grna_target`, `target_chr`, `target_start`, `target_end`, `vector_id`, `n_umis`, `n_nonzero`, `p_mito`. They are sceptre's names. Other formats use other names for the same things, and none is a standard: the IGVF consortium's pipeline calls the modalities `gene` and `guide` and the target `intended_target_name`, and pertpy's example data calls them `rna` and `gdo`. If a name reads wrongly to you, now is the time to say so.

</details>

## Example

The tree below is a real data file, `example/highmoi/screen.h5mu`: sceptre's
high-MOI example data, with 500 cells, 100 genes and 60 gRNAs. Open a group to
see what is in it, and an entry to see its first rows. The descriptions are
read from the specification's own files.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.screen_tree())
```

A file may have columns the format does not define, such as `response_name` in
the gene table here, which holds gene symbols. Software ignores columns it
does not know.

Two more example files are in `example/`: sceptre's low-MOI example data, and
a small made-up file that has every kind of column the format allows.

## Native reading

The format has no reader of its own. A data file is read with the standard
MuData library of each language, and what comes back is a standard object held
in memory: a `MultiAssayExperiment` in R and a `MuData` in Python.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
screen <- MuData::readH5MU("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
screen
```

The file's own entries, and the gRNA table:

```{r}
S4Vectors::metadata(screen)[c("perturb_seq_format", "dataset_id", "genome_build")]
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(screen[["grna"]]), 3)
```

## Python

```{python}
import mudata

screen = mudata.read_h5mu("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
print(screen)
```

The file's own entries, and the gRNA table:

```{python}
print({key: screen.uns[key] for key in ("perturb_seq_format", "dataset_id", "genome_build")})
print(screen["grna"].var.head(3))
```

:::

R shows each matrix as features × cells, and Python as cells × features. It is
the same stored matrix, which each language presents in its own convention.

### Reading from disk

For a file too large for memory, the counts stay on disk and are read one
feature at a time. Because counts are stored feature by feature, one gene is
one short read.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
counts <- HDF5Array::H5SparseMatrix("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu", "mod/rna/X")
dim(counts)                 # 100 500: features × cells, still on disk
sum(counts[1, ])            # 81: the counts of the first gene, read from the file
```

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
import h5py

with h5py.File("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu") as file:
    counts = file["mod/rna/X"]
    start, end = counts["indptr"][0:2]          # where the first gene's counts are
    print(counts["data"][start:end].sum())      # 81: one contiguous read
```

:::

### What a tool still has to check

A standard library does not know this format's rules, so a tool that reads a
data file makes two checks of its own afterwards. `check_screen()`, in the
folder `format/` of this repository, makes both on an object that has been read.

- **Refuse a file of a major version it does not know.**
- **Refuse a file in which one vector carries gRNAs with different targets.**

This is different from validating a file, which checks every rule and is
described in the next section. A tool that reads a file need not validate it.

### Writing

There is no standard writer either, and the standard libraries do not write a
conforming file by default: R's MuData writer, for instance, stores counts as
decimal numbers. A writer is a thin layer over the standard one that stores
counts as integers, feature by feature, and keeps to the allowed kinds of
column. `format/` has one for each language, `fmt_write_screen()` in R and
`write_screen()` in Python. They are temporary: they exist to test the format,
and the packages will write the files themselves.

## Validation

Four things check the format: a validator, a set of test files, a suite of
checks, and automatic runs of that suite on every change.

### What "conforms" means

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""The specification has {counts["all"]} numbered statements of three kinds.

| Kind | What it is about | How many | How it is checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| File rule | What a file contains | {counts["file"]} | By the validator, on the file alone. The validators check {"all of them" if counts["file_checked"] == counts["file"] else str(counts["file_checked"]) + " of them"} |
| Behaviour rule | What software reading or writing a file does | {counts["behaviour"]} | By a test where one exists: {counts["behaviour_tested"]} have one |
| Guidance | Advice to whoever writes files | {counts["guidance"]} | Not checked |
""")
```

A file **conforms** when it breaks no file rule. `SPEC.md` says beside each
statement how it is checked, and which ones nothing tests yet.

### The validator

`validate_screen()` takes a file on disk and returns the rules it breaks, with
where and why. It exists twice, in R and in Python (`format/`), and both read
the same machine-readable definitions (`spec/screen.json`). It uses no
analysis tool. Here it is on a test file in which a gRNA with a real target is
marked as a control:

```{python}
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "format")
import perturb_seq_data

problems = perturb_seq_data.validate_screen("conformance/invalid/screens/control_type_with_a_target.h5mu")
print(problems.to_string(index=False))
```

On a conforming file the result is empty.

### The conformance files

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""`conformance/` holds {conforming} files that conform and {broken} files that each
break one rule or a few. `conformance/cases.json` says, for every file, which
rules a validator must report. Both validators must report exactly those, no
more and no fewer. Someone writing another validator, or a reader, tests it
against the same files.""")
```

### The suite

`verify/run.sh` runs every check, in R and in Python, and prints a summary. The
counts below are from the run this page was rendered after.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.status({
    "conformance": "Both validators report exactly the expected rules on every conformance file. A few broken files, such as one with counts stored as decimal numbers, do not conform but must still be read correctly by the standard libraries, and are",
    "encodings": "Every kind of column, written by each language's standard library and read by the other's. The kinds the format allows come back correct. The kinds it forbids, such as true/false columns, do not, which is why they are forbidden",
    "independent-readers": "Tools that know nothing of this format read the example files: anndata and scanpy in Python, HDF5Array in R",
    "wide-index": "Files whose count matrices need 64-bit positions, which very large screens do. No test file is that large, so the limit is lowered for the test",
    "writers": "What a writer must do beyond producing a conforming file: a copy of a data file keeps the dataset's identifier and every modality",
}))
```

The two languages run different numbers of checks in some groups, because
each tests its own libraries.

### Automatic runs

The suite runs by itself on GitHub whenever a change is pushed to this folder,
on three fresh machines: Linux, macOS and Windows. Each installs only standard
libraries, then runs `verify/run.sh`. A failure on any of them marks the change
as failing. The current state and the history of runs are at the
[workflow's page](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/actions/workflows/perturb-seq-data-format.yml).

### At real size

The example files are small. Once, by hand, the format was run on a real large
screen: 207,324 cells, 13,135 genes and 13,077 gRNAs. Both languages wrote the
data to identical files of 5.7 GB, both validators passed them, and both read
them back, in memory and one gene at a time from disk. `scale-test/` has the
numbers.

### What is not tested

- Real data with a second measured modality, such as protein.
- A count matrix with more than about 2.1 billion nonzero counts, where
  positions no longer fit in 32 bits. The file layout for that case is tested
  at small size only.
- An implementation by someone else. One author wrote the specification and
  both validators.

## Open questions

Review is wanted on these most.

1. **Is anything missing that a real screen needs?** For gRNAs the format has a target, its position, an optional vector and an optional kind. It has no spacer sequence and no position of the gRNA itself yet, and it defines no annotation of genes, not even gene symbols. It holds gRNA counts, so a screen delivered only as gRNA calls has no place in it.
2. **Coordinates.** Target positions are 1-based with both ends included, as in GTF files, and a file with positions has to say which genome build they are in. Is that the right convention?
3. **Limits.** A gRNA has one target, and so does a vector carrying several gRNAs; a library that combines targets on one vector is refused. Targets are assumed to be on DNA. Are those limits acceptable for now?
4. **The matrix layout.** Counts are stored feature by feature, which suits fitting one gene at a time. Files from mapping pipelines and from scanpy are stored cell by cell. Should the format allow both and recommend one? The cost of converting a large file from one layout to the other has not been measured.
5. **What counts as data.** The format advises that a value some method computed, such as a cell-type label, a cluster or a score, is kept with the analysis that uses it and not in the data file. This is advice: a file that carries such a column still conforms, and sceptre does not put its own there. The count summaries `n_umis`, `n_nonzero` and `p_mito` are the exception the format itself defines. Other formats keep computed annotations in the cell table. Is this boundary the right one?
6. **The names.** Would you use `rna` and `grna`, `grna_target`, and the entry names in `uns`, or do the names of another format serve better?

<details class="fold">
<summary>What does not need review now</summary>

These can be added or changed later without breaking any file.

- **Optional columns not yet in the format:** spacer, the gRNA's own position, gene annotation (`RATIONALE.md`, planned additions).
- **The wording of individual rules.** The sorting into file rules, behaviour rules and guidance is meant to be final; the sentences are not.
- **Compression settings.** Software reading the files does not depend on them.
- **The code in `format/`.** The validators show that the rules can be checked in both languages; the writers there are temporary.
- **The comparisons with other formats** in `RATIONALE.md`, unless you know those formats and see an error.

</details>
